questions.stem: Which of the following forms India's 'Reserve Money' (M0)?

options.option_text: Currency with the public + demand deposits
Currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI

questions.explanation: M0 ('reserve money' / 'monetary base' / 'high-powered money') — the most liquid measure, what the RBI directly creates. M1 = M0 + demand deposits; M2 = M1 + post-office savings deposits; M3 = M1 + time deposits with banks ('broad money' — the most commonly reported aggregate). RBI targets broad money (M3) in its monetary policy framework.

questions.stem: India's demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes was announced on:
questions.explanation: PM Narendra Modi announced demonetisation of the then-existing ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes on 8 November 2016, effective midnight. New ₹500 and ₹2,000 notes were introduced. The ₹2,000 note was withdrawn from circulation in May 2023. Stated objectives — counter black money, fake currency, terror financing. Impact was contested in the RBI's 2017 annual report showing that 99.3 % of the demonetised notes were returned.

questions.stem: The 'e-Rupee' launched by the RBI (pilot in 2022) is an example of:
questions.explanation: CBDC — central-bank-issued digital currency, legal tender, centralised. Distinct from cryptocurrency (decentralised, private, volatile). The RBI's e-Rupee (digital rupee) comes in wholesale (e₹-W, for bank-to-bank settlement, pilot Nov 2022) and retail (e₹-R, for consumers, pilot Dec 2022) variants. China (e-CNY), Nigeria (e-Naira), Bahamas (Sand Dollar) are other early CBDC adopters.

questions.stem: Coins in India are minted by:
questions.explanation: Coins are minted under the Coinage Act 2011 by the Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India Ltd (SPMCIL) — under the Ministry of Finance. Four mints: Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Noida. The RBI distributes them and also has the sole right to ISSUE currency notes (printed at currency presses in Nashik, Dewas + BRBNMPL presses in Mysuru and Salboni).

questions.stem: The 'money multiplier' of an economy is approximately the reciprocal of:
questions.explanation: Basic money-multiplier model — if banks keep fraction 'r' (CRR) of deposits as reserves and lend the rest, the total money created from a new deposit is 1/r. If CRR = 4 %, the multiplier is 25 (ignoring other leakages like cash in hand). Real-world multipliers are lower due to cash preferences, excess reserves, and the SLR constraint. Still the simplest link between reserve ratio and broad-money growth.

questions.stem: 'Gresham's law' in monetary economics states that:

options.option_text: Bad money drives out good money from circulation

questions.explanation: Gresham's law (attributed to Sir Thomas Gresham, 16th c.) — 'Bad money drives out good' — when two currencies circulate at the same legal value but have different intrinsic values, people hoard the more valuable (good) one and spend the less valuable (bad) one. Classic case — when debased silver coins circulated alongside pure silver coins, pure ones disappeared from daily use.

questions.stem: The 'rupee' symbol ₹ — adopted by India in 2010 — was designed by:
questions.explanation: D. Udaya Kumar, a post-graduate from IIT Bombay's Industrial Design Centre, won the Government's open design competition in 2010; his ₹ glyph — a stylised fusion of the Devanagari letter 'र' (ra) and the Latin 'R', with two horizontal lines at top — was adopted by the Union Cabinet on 15 July 2010. Unicode code point U+20B9. India is one of the few countries whose currency symbol was picked via public competition.
